templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Despite sitting), passage-final clause; right subject is a part of the obvious noun (the fish’s eyes)
items.passage: The barreleye (Macropinna microstoma), an unusual deep-sea fish found throughout the northern Pacific, has a transparent, fluid-filled shield enclosing the top of its head. Despite sitting deep within this protective canopy, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the barreleye can rotate its two tubular eyes, so it can look straight up for prey or forward while feeding.
there are two tubular eyes that can rotate, letting the barreleye look straight up for prey or forward while feeding.
the barreleye’s two tubular eyes can rotate, letting the fish look straight up for prey or forward while feeding.
the rotation of the barreleye’s two tubular eyes lets the fish look straight up for prey or forward while feeding.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that sits deep within the protective shield on the fish’s head, which can only be the fish’s eyes, not the whole fish. Choice C places “the barreleye’s two tubular eyes” right after the phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the eyes.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun keeps every fact
A.why_wrong: “The barreleye” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the whole fish sits deep within the shield that covers its own head.

B.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

D.why_wrong: The head of the subject is “rotation,” so the sentence says that a movement, rather than the eyes, sits deep within the shield.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (barreleye fish, Macropinna microstoma, eyes that rotate inside a transparent head shield). No named researchers. Band 7 on the 37e5c794 (3.16) and 2dd1b8bf pattern: the opener fits only a part of the obvious noun, the right subject is a possessive built on that noun, and the hardest distractor (A) starts with the fish and keeps every fact. Options 19 to 21 words; key the shortest.
band7_moves: component key: only the eyes can sit within the shield, so the right subject is “the barreleye’s two tubular eyes,” a possessive built on the obvious noun (as silica glass’s atomic arrangement in 2dd1b8bf)
hardest distractor (A) starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact, failing only on what the opener can describe
the key is the only option opening with a possessive, so a student taught that possessive subjects dangle (recipe P) is drawn away from it
key noun (eyes) absent from the passage; recipes W, E, N

band7.why: Component key on the 2dd1b8bf pattern (the barreleye’s two tubular eyes), hardest distractor A starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact, plus E and N; key noun absent from the passage. Options run 19 to 21 words, longer than the 12 to 16 the spec suggests, but no option dies on an obvious fact.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Averaged for each location), passage-final clause; right subject is a property (walking speed)
items.passage: In a 1976 study, researchers Marc and Helen Bornstein timed pedestrians walking a fixed distance along the main streets of locations in several countries, ranging from small rural villages to metropolitan areas with populations in the millions. Averaged for each location, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the walking speed of the pedestrians rose steadily with the size of the local population.
the pedestrians walked faster and faster as the size of the local population increased.
the researchers found walking speed to rise steadily with the size of the local population.
there was a steady rise in walking speed as the size of the local population increased.
items.explanation: Only a quantity, such as a speed, can be averaged for each location. Choice A places “the walking speed of the pedestrians” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the speed.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun keeps every fact
B.why_wrong: “The pedestrians” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the pedestrians themselves were averaged for each location.

C.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the researchers
C.why_wrong: “The researchers” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the researchers were averaged for each location.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Bornstein and Bornstein 1976, “The pace of life”: walking speed rose with population size). Real study, known; only its core finding is stated. Band 7 on the fced396a (3.26) and 8b017d4e (3.27) pattern: “Averaged for each location” admits only a quantity, so the key is “the Y of X” while B starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact, and C copies the 3.27 move of offering the researchers as subject. Options 14 to 16 words; key not the longest.
band7_moves: property key: only a measured quantity can be “averaged for each location,” so the right subject is “the walking speed of the pedestrians” (the Y of X, as the HHI score of a market in fced396a)
hardest distractor (B) starts with the obvious noun, the pedestrians, and keeps every fact
a second wrong subject (the researchers) that looks like the safe reporting frame of 3.14 and 3.27
fresh opener (Averaged for each location) instead of the officials’ “Compared with that of”; recipes W, W, E

fixes: passage: “psychologists Marc and Helen Bornstein” to “researchers Marc and Helen Bornstein” (Helen Bornstein’s field not confirmed; neutral role word)

band7.why: Property key (“the walking speed of the pedestrians”) on the fced396a and 8b017d4e pattern; B starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact, C offers the researchers as in 3.27. Run is short (19 words), so it sits at the low end of band 7.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, passage-final clause
items.passage: Firefly squid (Watasenia scintillans) spend most of the year at considerable depths in the Sea of Japan, producing bioluminescent light from tiny specialized organs on their bodies. Rising toward the surface by the millions to spawn each spring, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Japan’s Toyama Bay fills with a blue glow from the squid, drawing crowds of visitors to the shore.
the squid’s light organs fill Japan’s Toyama Bay with a blue glow that draws crowds of visitors to the shore.
it is in Japan’s Toyama Bay that the squid create a blue glow, drawing crowds of visitors to the shore.
the squid fill Japan’s Toyama Bay with a blue glow that draws crowds of visitors to the shore.
items.explanation: The squid themselves are what rise toward the surface to spawn. Choice D places “the squid” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the squid.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the place
A.why_wrong: “Japan’s Toyama Bay” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the bay rises toward the surface to spawn.

B.why_wrong: The head of “the squid’s light organs” is “organs,” so the sentence says the light organs, rather than the squid, rise toward the surface to spawn.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (firefly squid spawning in Toyama Bay, Japan). No named researchers. Band 6: plain agent subject, recipes W, P, E; “to spawn” rules out the light organs as well as the bay. Key the shortest option.

band7.why: Plain agent key (the squid), the band-6 R3 pattern; W, P, E distractors, with “to spawn” killing the light organs quickly. Written to band 6.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, mid-sentence blank; right subject is a part of a building (its roof)
items.passage: Spanish-born Mexican architect Félix Candela specialized in roofs built from hyperbolic paraboloids, saddle-shaped surfaces whose double curvature makes them remarkably strong for their weight. A concrete shell only about four centimeters thick, ______ covers an open dining hall without a single interior column.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Candela’s use of this form at Los Manantiales, a restaurant in Mexico City,
the roof of Los Manantiales, a restaurant Candela designed in Mexico City,
Candela designed Los Manantiales, a restaurant in Mexico City, and its roof
Los Manantiales, a restaurant that Candela designed in Mexico City, has a roof that
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes a concrete shell about four centimeters thick, which can only be the restaurant’s roof. Choice B places “the roof of Los Manantiales” right after the phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the roof.

A.recipe: agent in possessive (P), wrong head noun
A.why_wrong: The head of “Candela’s use of this form” is “use,” so the sentence illogically says an architect’s use of a shape, rather than the roof, is a concrete shell four centimeters thick.

C.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the person
C.why_wrong: “Candela” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the architect himself is a concrete shell.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the whole building, with the part moved into the predicate
D.why_wrong: “Los Manantiales,” the restaurant, follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the restaurant is a concrete shell four centimeters thick, even as it says the restaurant has a roof; the shell is the roof, not the restaurant.

items.notes: Subject: arts, architecture (Félix Candela’s Los Manantiales restaurant, Xochimilco, 1958, a thin hyperbolic paraboloid shell). Band 6 as WAVE.md directs: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items, so the planned band 7 is written as a strong band 6. Moves kept from band 7: the right subject is a part of the obvious noun (the roof of Los Manantiales), and two wrong subjects are the building and its architect. Key not the longest. Option D (the restaurant as subject) rebuilt in review on the fced396a pattern (“a less concentrated market will have an HHI score that”): the restaurant “has a roof that” covers the hall, so the sentence itself separates the building from its shell and the opener can only describe the roof.

fixes: option D rebuilt from “Los Manantiales, a restaurant that Candela designed in Mexico City in 1958,” to “Los Manantiales, a restaurant that Candela designed in Mexico City, has a roof that”: the old D was defensible by metonymy (thin-shell buildings are routinely called shells), and the kill leaned on the verb, not the modifier; the new D follows fced396a D and states the roof separately, so only B fits; why_wrong and notes updated

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 with a part-of-building key (the roof) and the whole building as the hardest distractor.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family options; singular head behind stacked plural interveners and a relative clause with its own plural verb
items.passage: Movile Cave in southeastern Romania remained isolated from the surface for millions of years. The primary source of energy for the cave’s dozens of species of spiders, leeches, and other invertebrates, which never encounter sunlight, ______ a floating mat of bacteria that extract energy from hydrogen sulfide dissolved in the groundwater.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “source,” so the singular verb “is” agrees with it. The plural nouns in between (“species,” “spiders,” “leeches,” “invertebrates”) and the plural verb “encounter” belong to the phrase and clause that describe the source.

A.recipe: wrong number (plural present), agrees with the nearest nouns
A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “source.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular subject “source.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “source.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Movile Cave, Romania, an ecosystem fed by sulfur-oxidizing bacteria). No named researchers. Band 6: head “source” 22 words before the blank, four plural attractors and a relative clause (which never encounter sunlight) whose own verb is plural; the complement “a floating mat” is singular so “is” reads cleanly.

band7.why: Meets the section 5 R1 settings: four plural attractors, a relative clause with its own plural verb (encounter), head 22 words before the blank, as in 0fe5ce68. Written to band 6; singular head is the weaker direction, but it reads band 7.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb after a dash-enclosed participial interrupter
items.passage: For centuries, residents of the Egyptian town of Oxyrhynchus discarded unwanted documents on rubbish mounds at the desert’s edge, where the arid climate preserved them. Those mounds—excavated by British scholars Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt beginning in 1896—______ hundreds of thousands of papyrus fragments, including lost poems by Sappho.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Those mounds” still needs a main verb when the interruption between the dashes ends. The finite verb “yielded” supplies it, completing the sentence.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: The participle “yielding” leaves “Those mounds” without a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
C.why_wrong: “Having yielded” is a participle, not a main verb, so the sentence remains a fragment.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
D.why_wrong: The infinitive “to yield” cannot serve as the main verb of “Those mounds,” so the sentence is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Oxyrhynchus rubbish mounds, excavated by Grenfell and Hunt from 1896). Real, well-known facts only. Band 6 on the 3.13 pattern: the dash pair holds a past participle (excavated) that can pass for the main verb, and the blank sits 15 words after its subject.

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 on the 3.13 pattern with a dash interrupter holding a past participle.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, third verb of a compound predicate after a dash interrupter with its own finite verb
items.passage: Egyptian writer Taha Hussein lost his sight in early childhood, studied at Cairo’s al-Azhar University and subsequently in France, and, in his autobiography The Days—a book whose first volume appeared in the 1920s—______ his village upbringing in the third person, as though writing about someone else.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Taha Hussein” has a series of past-tense verbs joined by “and”: “lost,” “studied,” and a third verb that the blank must supply. The finite past-tense verb “described” completes the series.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: After “and,” the series needs a third past-tense verb to match “lost” and “studied”; the participle “describing” leaves it incomplete.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to describe” cannot complete a series of finite verbs, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having described” is a participle, not a finite verb, so it cannot be the third verb in the series.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Taha Hussein, The Days, told in the third person). Band 6 as WAVE.md directs: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official items, so the planned band 7 is written as a strong band 6. Moves: the blank is the third verb of a series begun 25 words earlier, and the dash interrupter holds its own finite verb (appeared) right before the blank, as the praised clause does in 2.1.

band7.why: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 with the blank as the third verb of a series begun 25 words earlier and a finite verb inside the dash interrupter.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical-verb options; singular head behind a title gloss and an appositive with plural nouns
items.passage: Nubian musician Hamza El Din spent his childhood in a village later submerged beneath the reservoir of Egypt’s Aswan High Dam. The title composition of Escalay (The Water Wheel), one of several albums he recorded on the oud, ______ the steady, creaking rhythm of the ox-driven waterwheels that once irrigated Nubian farmland.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “composition,” so the singular verb “captures” agrees with it. The plural noun “albums” in the appositive describes the album Escalay, not the subject.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “capture” does not agree with the singular subject “composition.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are capturing” does not agree with the singular subject “composition.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have captured” does not agree with the singular subject “composition.”

items.notes: Subject: arts, music (Hamza El Din’s 1971 oud album Escalay and the Nubian water wheel). Medium: head “composition” 14 words before the blank, with plural “albums” in the appositive as the attractor.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid, singular possessor and plural possessed noun
items.passage: Bayanihan, a Filipino tradition of communal cooperation, is often captured in one striking image: a house in motion. When a family relocates, dozens of the ______ hoist its entire house onto sturdy bamboo poles and transport the structure to a new location.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The neighbors belong to one family (“a family relocates” and “its house”), so the singular possessive “family’s” is needed. “Neighbors” is a plain plural (dozens of them) that owns nothing, so it takes no apostrophe.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Neighbor’s” is a possessive, but the neighbors do not own anything in the sentence; the plain plural “neighbors” is needed.

B.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor, wrong possessor number
B.why_wrong: “Families” has no apostrophe to show possession and is plural, though the text describes a single family.

C.why_wrong: “Families’” is a plural possessive, but only one family is relocating (“a family,” “its house”).

items.notes: Subject: social science, Filipino culture (bayanihan, neighbors carrying a family’s house on bamboo poles). Number cues: “a family” before the blank and “its house” after it; “dozens of” for the plural neighbors.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (In jotting down), mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Essays in Idleness (Tsurezuregusa), composed in Japan around 1330 by the Buddhist monk Yoshida Kenkō, ranges over subjects from friendship to the beauty of impermanence. In jotting down observations on whatever came to mind, ______ in a loose, wandering style that later Japanese essayists would imitate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the observations of Kenkō were recorded
items.explanation: A person is the one who jots down observations. Choice A places “Kenkō” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the writer.

B.why_wrong: The head of “Kenkō’s essays” is “essays,” so the sentence illogically says the essays jotted down observations.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

D.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
D.why_wrong: “The observations” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the observations jotted themselves down.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Yoshida Kenkō’s Essays in Idleness, about 1330). Medium: short, clear opener describing a person; recipes P, E, V.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family options; singular head behind a relative clause with a plural subject and verb
items.passage: Builders in Yemen’s Hadhramaut valley have constructed homes from sun-dried mud brick for centuries. The walled city of Shibam, whose approximately 500 tower houses reach heights of up to eleven stories, ______ frequently described as “the Manhattan of the desert.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “city,” so the singular verb “is” agrees with it. The plural “tower houses” and its verb “reach” belong to the clause that describes the city.

A.recipe: wrong number (plural present), agrees with the nearest noun
A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “city.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “city.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular subject “city.”

items.notes: Subject: history and architecture (Shibam, Yemen, mud-brick tower houses). Medium: a whose-clause with plural “tower houses,” its plural verb “reach” and plural “heights” and “stories” sits between head and blank.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Made up of), mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Tomás Rivera’s experiences growing up in a family of Mexican American migrant farmworkers informed his celebrated 1971 book …And the Earth Did Not Devour Him. Made up of linked short stories and brief vignettes, ______ follows an unnamed boy as he struggles to reconstruct a forgotten year of his life.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Rivera published this book in 1971, and it
the publication of this book by Rivera
items.explanation: Only the book can be made up of short stories and vignettes. Choice B places “this book by Rivera” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the book.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the author
A.why_wrong: “Rivera” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the writer himself is made up of short stories and vignettes.

C.why_wrong: The head of the subject is “publication,” so the sentence says an event, rather than the book, is made up of stories and follows a boy.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W) after a prepositional phrase
D.why_wrong: The subject of the clause is “Rivera,” so the sentence still says the writer is made up of short stories and vignettes.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Tomás Rivera’s 1971 book of linked stories and vignettes, the lost year). Medium: plain thing as the right subject; recipes W, N, W.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, -ing result phrase after a complete clause
items.passage: After a glass of wine is swirled, droplets gradually accumulate on the interior of the glass and trickle back down. Because alcohol evaporates more quickly than water from the thin film of wine coating the glass, the film’s surface tension increases and draws additional liquid upward, ______ a ridge that eventually collapses into these “tears.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause is already complete (“the film’s surface tension increases and draws additional liquid upward”). The participle “forming” begins a phrase that describes the result of that pull.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (past)
A.why_wrong: “Formed” would be a second main verb after the comma with no subject or conjunction, which is ungrammatical.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (past perfect)
B.why_wrong: “Had formed” is a finite verb with no subject of its own, so it cannot follow the complete clause after a comma.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (present)
C.why_wrong: “Form” is a finite verb with no subject of its own; after the comma it leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: physical science (tears of wine, the Marangoni effect). No named researchers. Medium on the 2.9 pattern: the result phrase follows a compound predicate (increases and draws).

items.subtype: Tense, simple present for an ongoing, general process
items.passage: Nighttime visitors to the crater of Kawah Ijen, a volcano in East Java, Indonesia, can witness an unusual phenomenon: brilliant blue flames. The volcano continuously ______ sulfurous gases that ignite on contact with oxygen in the atmosphere, producing an electric-blue glow.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes something that happens now and on an ongoing basis (“can witness,” “continuously,” “ignite”). The simple present “releases” fits this ongoing process.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: “Had released” places the action before some other past event, but the text describes a present, ongoing process.

C.why_wrong: “Would have released” describes something that did not happen, which conflicts with the visible flames described in the present.

D.why_wrong: “Will have been releasing” refers to a point in the future, but the text describes what the volcano does now.

items.notes: Subject: earth science (Kawah Ijen, blue flames from burning sulfur gases, East Java). No named researchers. Easy: present cues in the same sentence (continuously, ignite).

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement, subject pronoun for a named person
items.passage: Economist Sam Peltzman examined US traffic fatality data from before and after federal law began requiring safety equipment such as seat belts in new cars. In a 1975 paper, ______ argued that drivers who felt safer tended to take more risks, offsetting part of the regulations’ intended benefit.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person who wrote the 1975 paper is Sam Peltzman, a single man named in the previous sentence. The singular pronoun “he” refers to him.

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” does not agree with the singular antecedent “Sam Peltzman.”

B.why_wrong: The plural demonstrative “those” does not refer clearly to Peltzman and does not agree with a single person.

D.why_wrong: “Both” refers to two people or things, but only one economist is named.

items.notes: Subject: social science, economics (Peltzman 1975, risk compensation after auto safety regulation). Real, well-known claim only. Easy: one named person as the only possible arguer.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement, subject pronoun for a named person
items.passage: Cameroonian artist Francis Bebey worked as a radio journalist, a novelist, and a classical guitarist. In the 1970s and early 1980s, ______ recorded experimental songs that combined drum machines and synthesizers with traditional African instruments such as the sanza, a thumb piano.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person who recorded the songs is Francis Bebey, a single man named in the previous sentence. The singular pronoun “he” refers to him.

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” does not agree with the singular antecedent “Francis Bebey.”

C.why_wrong: The plural demonstrative “those” has no plural antecedent and does not agree with a single musician.

D.why_wrong: “Some” refers to an unspecified group, but the text is about one musician.

items.notes: Subject: arts, music (Francis Bebey’s experimental recordings of the 1970s and early 1980s, drum machines and the sanza). Easy: antecedent is the subject of the previous sentence; the nouns between are singular roles.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family options; singular head with a short of-phrase, no number clash
items.passage: Established in the fifth century CE in present-day Bihar, India, the monastery of Nalanda ______ one of the most influential centers of Buddhist scholarship in Asia, attracting students and teachers from as far away as China.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “monastery,” and the opening phrase places it in the past. The singular past verb “was” agrees with the subject.

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular subject “monastery.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “monastery.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “monastery.”

items.notes: Subject: history (Nalanda, Buddhist center of learning in Bihar). Easy: head “monastery” three words before the blank, with only the singular name “Nalanda” between.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical-verb options; singular head after each, no intervener
items.passage: In the temple town of Nathdwara in Rajasthan, India, artists create pichwais, elaborate cloth paintings displayed behind the temple’s devotional image of the Hindu god Krishna. Each pichwai ______ an episode from Krishna’s life or a celebration from the temple’s religious calendar.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Each pichwai” is singular, so the singular verb “shows” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “show” does not agree with the singular subject “Each pichwai.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are showing” does not agree with the singular subject “Each pichwai.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have shown” does not agree with the singular subject “Each pichwai.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (pichwai paintings at Nathdwara). Easy: “Each” plus a singular noun right before the blank; the plural “pichwais” sits in the previous sentence.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb after a short participial phrase
items.passage: Giant tube worms, which cluster around hydrothermal vents on the deep seafloor, have no mouth and no digestive system. Instead, bacteria living inside each worm ______ chemicals from the vent water into nutrients that feed their host.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “bacteria” needs a main verb. The finite present-tense verb “convert” supplies it, completing the sentence.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: The participle “converting” leaves “bacteria” without a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
C.why_wrong: “Having converted” is a participle, not a main verb, so the sentence remains a fragment.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
D.why_wrong: The infinitive “to convert” cannot serve as the main verb of “bacteria,” so the sentence is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (giant tube worms at hydrothermal vents and their symbiotic bacteria). No named researchers. Easy: main-verb slot after a short subject.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, first verb of a compound predicate
items.passage: Slow lorises, nocturnal primates that inhabit the forests of South and Southeast Asia, are among the few mammals capable of producing venom. A threatened slow loris ______ its arms above its head and licks a gland on each upper arm, combining the gland’s oily secretion with its saliva.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “A threatened slow loris” needs a main verb, and “raises” pairs with the second verb “licks.” The finite present-tense verb “raises” completes the sentence.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: “Raising” is not a finite verb, so it cannot pair with “licks” as the main verb of the subject.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to raise” cannot serve as the main verb of “A threatened slow loris.”

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having raised” is a participle and cannot pair with “licks” as the main verb.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (slow loris venom, brachial gland secretion mixed with saliva). No named researchers. Easy: the parallel verb “licks” confirms the finite form.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: full 2 x 2 grid, singular possessor and plural noun
items.passage: Pakistani architect Yasmeen Lari spent decades designing large modernist buildings before devoting herself to disaster relief. Many of the ______ for families whose homes were destroyed by floods are built from bamboo, lime, and mud, materials that are inexpensive and available locally.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The shelters belong to one architect, Yasmeen Lari, so the singular possessive “architect’s” is needed. “Shelters” is a plain plural (“Many of the”) that owns nothing, so it takes no apostrophe.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Shelter’s” is a possessive, but the shelters do not own anything in the sentence.

C.why_wrong: “Architects” lacks the apostrophe that shows the shelters belong to the architect.

D.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor, needless apostrophe on the plural
D.why_wrong: “Architects” lacks the possessive apostrophe, and “shelter’s” wrongly adds one to a plain plural.

items.notes: Subject: arts, architecture (Yasmeen Lari’s low-cost bamboo, lime and mud shelters). Easy: one named architect as the possessor; “Many of the” cues the plain plural.

items.subtype: Tense, past perfect for an action completed before a dated past event
items.passage: In 2000, miners excavating Mexico’s Naica mine broke into a cavern containing enormous gypsum crystals, some more than ten meters long. By then, the crystals ______ gradually for hundreds of thousands of years in heated, mineral-rich groundwater.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “By then” refers back to 2000, when the miners broke into the cavern, and the growing happened before that moment. The past perfect “had grown” shows an action completed before another past event.

A.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
A.why_wrong: “Grow” is present tense, but the growing took place before a past event in 2000.

B.recipe: future where past perfect is needed
B.why_wrong: “Will grow” refers to the future, but the growing had already happened by 2000.

C.why_wrong: “Are growing” describes something happening now, not something completed before 2000.

items.notes: Subject: earth science (Naica Cave of the Crystals, giant gypsum crystals found by miners in 2000). No named people. Easy: explicit cue “By then” pointing to a dated past event.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive of purpose after a complete clause
items.passage: When a container of mixed nuts is shaken, the largest nuts typically end up on top, a tendency known as the Brazil nut effect. Physicists have developed computer simulations of vibrating granular materials ______ why larger particles migrate upward.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “Physicists have developed computer simulations of vibrating granular materials” is already complete. The infinitive “to explain” begins a phrase that gives the purpose of the simulations.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (present)
B.why_wrong: “Explains” is a finite verb with no subject of its own, so it cannot follow the complete clause.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (past)
C.why_wrong: “Explained” would be a second main verb with no subject or conjunction, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (present perfect)
D.why_wrong: “Have explained” is a finite verb with no subject of its own, so it cannot follow the complete clause.

items.notes: Subject: physical science (the Brazil nut effect in shaken granular mixtures). No named researchers. Easy: purpose infinitive after a complete clause.

items.subtype: Tense, simple past for a dated past event
items.passage: Until 1967, motorists in Sweden drove on the left side of the road, even though neighboring Norway and Finland had long since adopted right-hand traffic. Then, at 5:00 a.m. on September 3 of that year, vehicles throughout the country ______ to the right.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The change happened at a specific time in the past, September 3, 1967, and the earlier verb (“drove”) is also past. The simple past “switched” fits this dated event.

A.recipe: present simple where past is needed
A.why_wrong: “Switches” is present tense, but the switch happened on a specific date in 1967.

B.why_wrong: “Will switch” refers to the future, but the event took place in 1967.

D.recipe: present perfect beside a dated past
D.why_wrong: “Has switched” is not used with a specific past time such as “at 5:00 a.m. on September 3 of that year.”

items.notes: Subject: social history (Dagen H, Sweden’s switch to right-hand traffic on 3 September 1967). Easy: explicit dated cue in the same sentence.
